title: Logan Star Dafne Keen Reveals Childhood Cocaine Offer; Hugh Jackman Safeguarded Her On‑Set Hours
body:
The former “Logan” child star has opened up about a dark side of Hollywood that she encountered as a pre‑teen, saying she was once handed cocaine at an industry party. In a candid interview on the “Inside of You” podcast, 21‑year‑old Dafne Keen recounted the unsettling offer and praised Hugh Jackman for protecting her well‑being on set, insisting that the veteran actor made sure her working hours were never exploited. Her revelations shed new light on the pressures faced by young performers and have reignited discussion about safeguarding minors in the entertainment business.

Keen first captured global attention in 2017 when she portrayed the ferocious mutant Laura /X‑23 alongside Hugh Jackman in the critically acclaimed “Logan.” The role earned her a BAFTA nomination and cemented her status as a breakout talent. Since then, she has built a diverse résumé that includes the sci‑fi series “The Peripheral” and the thriller “The Stranger.” Yet despite a career that appears to be on an upward trajectory, the actress says the glamour of early fame was marred by moments that left her feeling vulnerable and out of place.

During the podcast, Keen described how, at just 11 years old, she was invited to a Hollywood gathering where an adult handed her a line of cocaine, asking if she wanted to try it. She recalled the confusion and fear that accompanied the incident, noting that she immediately declined and left the party. “I was just a kid who wanted to be on a set and do my job,” she said. “Seeing that kind of thing made me realize how quickly the industry can blur the lines between work and reckless behavior.” Her account aligns with a growing chorus of former child actors who have spoken about exposure to drugs, alcohol, and other adult environments at an age when they should be protected.

Hugh Jackman’s role in Keen’s early career extends beyond their on‑screen chemistry. Keen praised the Australian star for his vigilance, explaining that he routinely checked on her schedule and made sure she was not overworked or placed in compromising situations. “He would come over during breaks, ask if I was okay, and remind the crew that I was still a kid,” she said. Jackman’s mentorship, she added, set a standard for how senior actors can act as guardians for younger colleagues. Industry insiders note that such advocacy is not universally practiced, and Keen’s testimony may prompt studios to formalize mentorship responsibilities for veteran cast members.

The actress’s disclosure arrives at a time when the entertainment sector is under heightened scrutiny for its treatment of minors. Recent high‑profile investigations have revealed lax oversight on set, inadequate mental‑health support, and insufficient enforcement of child‑labor laws. Advocacy groups are calling for stricter regulations, including mandatory on‑set child welfare officers and clearer protocols for reporting inappropriate behavior. Keen’s story adds a personal dimension to these policy debates, illustrating how a single lapse—such as an adult offering a drug to a child—can have lasting repercussions.

While Keen’s revelations are unsettling, they also underscore her resilience and the protective network that helped her navigate a treacherous industry. She emphasized that the experience, though harrowing, motivated her to become an outspoken advocate for safer working conditions for young talent. “If sharing this helps even one kid avoid a similar situation, it’s worth it,” she said.

Looking ahead, the conversation sparked by Keen’s interview is likely to influence both studio practices and public perception. As more former child actors step forward, the industry may be compelled to adopt comprehensive safeguarding measures, ensuring that the next generation of stars can focus on their craft without fear of exploitation. For Keen, the hope is that her voice contributes to a cultural shift where the well‑being of young performers is no longer an afterthought but a foundational priority.
